articles.title: Mass badger cull ruled out by Welsh government after speculation
articles.summary: Plaid Cymru ministers rule out mass badger cull as part of new plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis.
articles.content:
Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd MS, said bovine TB remained "one of the most serious animal health challenges facing Wales".

"We will not stand by while farmers face uncertainty and anxiety, nor will we pursue a mass non-selective cull," he added.

"Instead, we will be taking evidence-based and science-led action, incorporating the three pillars of cattle, people and wildlife.

"Farmers and the public will rightly judge us on whether we prevent disease and reduce its impact, even when the decisions are difficult."

NFU Cymru president Abi Reader said farmers needed to see action quickly on measures promised in the government's announcement.

"Going for a mass badger cull was never going to be on the cards - that's quite a seismic change," she said.

"There's certainly this leaning towards what we call a trap, test and remove [programme] - that's really good, but we need to see that starting and actually being acted on."

"That's what farmers will have wanted to see today from this statement," she said.

"For those farmers who are right in the eye of the storm - and have been dealing with TB for a very long time - I think they were hoping they would have seen something that would have given them more hope for the future."

Ian Rickman, president of the Farmers' Union of Wales (FUW), said it was "positive to note that targeted and proportionate action will now be taken on TB in wildlife where evidence supports this approach".

He said the loss of 92,000 cattle under bovine TB meant it was now time to intensify co-operation between groups including the industry, the veterinary profession and government.

RSPCA Cymru said it "cautiously welcomed the majority of today's statement".

"However, the fight has not been won yet. The killing of wildlife is not off the table, which is a concern," said Billie-Jade Thomas, the charity's senior public affairs manager.

"The Welsh government must prioritise a science-led, cattle-focussed approach towards combating this awful disease," she added.

Nigel Palmer, chief executive of The Badger Trust said he was "disappointed".

"It's good that the mass cull has been ruled out [but] we still don't see any need on a targeted or any other basis to bring badgers back into the equation.

"Wales has led for so long on bovine TB and actually has really good performance figures," he said.
articles.reasoning: The Welsh government ruling out a mass badger cull to tackle bovine tuberculosis represents a positive, science-led, and humane approach to disease control that balances animal welfare and agricultural needs. This decision has broad significance for public health, farming communities, and wildlife conservation in Wales. The article provides sufficient context on the disease challenge, stakeholder reactions, and alternative strategies, making it a substantive and meaningful environmental and animal welfare story.

articles.personality_presentation:

**What happened** – The Welsh government announced it will not use a large-scale badger cull to control bovine TB. Instead, they plan to rely on science-based methods that focus on cattle, people, and wildlife. This decision was shared by Llyr Gruffydd, a government minister responsible for rural matters.

**Impact** – This choice is important because it avoids killing many badgers, an animal linked to the spread of TB but also protected and valued by the public. Farmers and animal groups have responded positively, as the plan aims to balance keeping farms healthy while protecting wildlife. The government’s approach also means using testing and removing infected animals, rather than broad culling.

**What's next step** – The government will work with farmers, vets, and others to put these plans into action. Programs like trap, test, and remove for badgers may start soon. Everyone will watch closely to see if these methods reduce TB and help farmers feel more confident.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Wales chooses a careful, science-driven strategy to fight bovine TB without a mass badger cull, aiming to protect both farms and wildlife.

articles.title: Sunscreen, sweat and permastank: the science of stubborn laundry stains
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most stubborn laundry stains are a chemistry problem, and the fix depends on matching the treatment to the molecule. Fats need fat-digesting enzymes, plant pigments break down under ultraviolet light, and mineral buildup dissolves in mild acid. Get the pairing wrong, and the stain can set permanently. Eric Thompson, […]
The post Sunscreen, sweat and permastank: the science of stubborn laundry stains first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Most stubborn laundry stains are a chemistry problem, and the fix depends on matching the treatment to the molecule. Fats need fat-digesting enzymes, plant pigments break down under ultraviolet light, and mineral buildup dissolves in mild acid. Get the pairing wrong, and the stain can set permanently. Eric Thompson, a former management consultant near Seattle who moderates the r/laundry forum on Reddit, has seen it happen. “If you pour vinegar on a burrito grease stain on white nylon, you now have orange nylon for eternity,” he said. “Acids bind colour to dye sites on nylon.”

His forum, with roughly 995,000 members, has become a clearinghouse for evidence-based fixes, and Thompson’s long technical guides on enzymes and citric acid rinses are among its most cited posts. “I don’t do hacks,” he says. “What I do is: ‘Let’s use biotech and green chemistry and the magic of water and time to gently take care of our clothes.'” The payoff goes beyond clean shirts. Clothes that last longer need replacing less often, which saves money and cuts textile waste.

Before trying any of the methods below, check care labels, follow safety instructions on household chemicals, and never combine products without confirming it’s safe. Most of these techniques are designed for cotton and polyester.

Enzymes and stubborn laundry stains

Lipases for cooking oil

Enzymes are the “bio” in biological detergents, and each type targets a different molecule. For grease from cooking oil, the enzyme to look for is lipase, which breaks down fats. Many detergents contain it, though packaging often lists only “enzymes,” so checking the manufacturer’s ingredient information can help.

Clare Mahon, a professor of polymer chemistry at Durham University whose lab has partnered with a major detergent maker on laundry research, recommends a pretreatment first: a paste of baking soda and water applied to the oily patch for about an hour. “Fats or oils contain ester linkages and that mixture can hydrolyse those,” she said, meaning the paste breaks the bonds down with water. “Then you get water-soluble products that can then be removed from the fabric.” Speed matters here. Over time, the lipids in oil oxidize and link together in ways baking soda can’t undo, “so the stains can be really persistent,” Mahon said.

DNase for gym clothes that won’t stop smelling

Workout gear that smells clean out of the wash but sour once it warms up has a nickname online: permastank. The culprit is a buildup of body oils and bacteria. One enzyme rarely found in standard detergents, deoxyribonuclease, or DNase, targets extracellular DNA, a material that has no smell itself but helps glue other grime to fabric. Steve Brown, a product designer in Sydney, ran into the problem with his Brazilian jiujitsu gear before developing a DNase-based booster. “I just couldn’t get the smell out of my rash guards; I had to throw a couple of them out,” he said.

Solvents, sunlight and acids

Oil-based solvents for bike grease

Black grease from a bike chain behaves differently from cooking oil. Mahon suggests spraying it with a light oil-based solvent and leaving it for about 10 minutes before washing. “Because it’s a more oily organic solvent, it can release the residue from the fabric a bit more, then the surfactants are able to lift it up in the wash,” she said. Surfactants are the molecules in detergent that bind to dirt and make it water-soluble, which is why an enzyme stain remover alone can’t replace detergent.

Sunlight for tomato sauce

Red sauce stains often get their color from lycopene, a pigment whose chemical bonds break down under UV light. After pretreating any grease with dish soap and washing as usual, drying the garment outside can fade lingering orange marks completely, even on an overcast day.

Citric acid for armpit stains and rough towels

Yellowed, stiff underarm patches come from a combination of sweat and deodorant, and Mahon calls them “a nightmare.” Soaking the area in water and citric acid can help dissolve aluminum deposits left by antiperspirant, though it can take several washes. Oxygen-based stain removers can help too, but leaving them on too long can lighten colored fabric.

Citric acid also helps with towels that dry scratchy, especially in homes without a tumble dryer. Stiffness often comes from using too much detergent, hard water, or both. Fabric softener isn’t the answer, since it coats fibers and reduces absorbency. Thompson prefers a rinse with dissolved citric acid in the softener compartment. “I am a huge proponent of using citric acid in the rinse,” he said. It binds to the calcium in hard water and neutralizes the alkaline pH that detergent leaves behind. Shaking towels sharply before hanging them also helps lift the fibers.

A repeat cycle for sunscreen

Sunscreen stains are among the hardest to shift. Many come from chemical UV filters such as avobenzone, which reacts with metal ions in water that then oxidize into a yellow mark. A rust stain remover can reverse the oxidation, but the metal stays in the fabric, and the stain can return as it dries. Thompson’s approach is a cycle of “pretreating, waiting, washing, rust-removing, and then washing again.”

Machine care and the last-resort deep clean

Cleaning the washer itself

A smelly washing machine will pass its odor on to everything in it. Manufacturers recommend a monthly cleaning cycle on the hottest setting, wiping out the rubber door seal, and periodically emptying and rinsing the drain pump filter, which collects lint, plastic, paper, and residue.

Polyquat spots

Some mystery marks appear only after washing. These are often polyquat stains, caused by polyquaterniums, polymers found in hair products, contact lens solution and children’s bubble mix. In the wash, they attract dirt and dye to the fabric, which effectively turns that patch into a color-catcher sheet, Mahon explained. Color-remover products can sometimes help, but they don’t work on indigo, so a polyquat spot that picked up dye from jeans is likely permanent.

Thompson’s “spa day”

For persistent odors and dinginess, Thompson’s forum is known for a long, enzyme-powered soak he calls a spa day. Items soak in water with a measured amount of enzyme detergent, held at around 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for several hours, before a regular wash; he also adds household ammonia for degreasing. Ammonia must never be mixed with chlorine bleach, since the combination releases a toxic gas. “It’s incumbent on all of us to keep textiles in the productive-use space as long as possible,” Thompson said. “Spa day is the last-ditch effort to do so when previous care has failed.”

None of this needs to become a weekly routine. Overwashing wears out fabric, and shorter cycles at lower temperatures use less energy. Thompson calls a regular mixed load “good enough” for most days, and Mahon thinks the bigger risk may be overthinking it. “To be honest with you, most people’s clothes aren’t actually that dirty,” she said. The chemistry becomes useful on the days a favorite shirt seems ruined, when knowing which molecule caused the stain can decide whether it goes back in the drawer or into the trash.

articles.title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
articles.summary: Once seen as a car for elderly, rural people, tiny cars are being embraced by a younger demographic.
articles.content:
Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.

"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.

In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.

In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16, external. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.

Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.

In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.

"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the growing adoption of tiny, low-speed electric cars across Europe, especially among younger people. This shift promotes sustainable, low-impact urban and rural mobility, reducing emissions and traffic congestion. The story provides concrete data on rising sales and regulatory frameworks, showing meaningful societal and environmental benefits.
articles.personality_title: Tiny electric cars gain popularity among European teens
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Small electric cars, once mostly used by older people in rural areas, are now becoming popular with younger drivers in Europe. These tiny vehicles are classified as motorised quadri-cycles, similar to four-wheel mopeds, and have different age limits for driving depending on the country.

**What happened** – Selena Buse, a 16-year-old from rural France, drives a Citroën Ami, a tiny electric car that can be driven from age 14 in France with basic training. Teenagers like Selena now make up about 25% of mini-car buyers. Sales of these cars have doubled in five years across Europe, with France seeing registrations rise from 13,000 in 2019 to 25,000 last year.

**Impact** – These small cars help young people travel independently in areas where public transport is limited. They also reduce traffic speeds and lower pollution since they are electric and slow-moving. The Ami’s unique design has changed how people see tiny cars, making them trendy among young drivers.

**What’s next step** – As more young people choose these cars, sales are expected to keep growing. This could encourage cities and countries to support electric micro-mobility with better rules and infrastructure, making travel easier and cleaner.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Tiny electric cars like the Citroën Ami are giving young Europeans a new, eco-friendly way to get around, especially outside big cities.

articles.personality_title: Making Christmas greener: simple steps to help the planet this holiday season
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Christmas holiday season is a time when many people celebrate with decorations, gifts, and special meals. However, these activities can create a lot of waste and increase pollution, affecting the environment.

**What happened** – As the holidays approach, experts and environmental groups are sharing ideas on how to make Christmas more eco-friendly. They discuss whether using real or plastic Christmas trees is better for nature and suggest easy actions everyone can take to lower their carbon footprint during the festivities.
